answer:
Viability: Weak-to-moderate and unproven. The path to revenue is clear in structure (a $9/month SaaS subscription with a free tier), but evidence of willingness to pay is thin: 1 paying customer out of 12 trial users (about 8%) and $27 in total revenue. The pain point is real but small by the team's own admission ('small per day'), which is the classic risk for a subscription priced against a low-urgency problem. Vendors already have free alternatives (paper, spreadsheets) and incumbents with offline modes, tax features and, critically, integrated card payments, which many vendors already use at the stall. Without payment processing, Ledgerleaf sits beside the core transaction rather than inside it, so it is a nice-to-have bookkeeping layer vs. a must-have system of record. Payment integration is where incumbents monetize (processing margin) and where lock-in comes from; planning it with only $3,500 of contract work looks optimistic given compliance and integration complexity.

Unit economics and revenue model: $9/month is cheap, so a vendor needs little persuasion, but it also caps scale. The plan's own local math yields about $19,400 ARR from 180 vendors, which is not a sustainable business and would not cover even modest salaries. Seasonality is a major unaddressed issue: many markets run 6-9 months, so churn or pauses will cut effective annual revenue below the 12x$9 assumption. The free tier (one market day per week of history) is confusing and may give away the core value to the majority who sell one day weekly. The market-manager reporting revenue stream is untested speculation and should not be counted. CAC is unmeasured; in-person, one-by-one market visits are labor-intensive and, at $9/month, payback could be long.

Scalability: Nationally the software scales cheaply, but the go-to-market does not: acquisition is physical, local, and relationship-driven. Market associations could be a real distribution lever if validated, but that is a hypothesis. The TAM is built top-down from an unverified 30 vendors/market average, then a guessed one-third 'serious' share; even taken at face value, 85,000 vendors at $9/month is about $9M/year, a small market, and the realistic serviceable share is far lower. Expansion into adjacent segments (craft fairs, food trucks, pop-ups) is not discussed but would be the logical way to widen the opportunity. No proprietary technology or data moat exists; the team concedes a larger provider could replicate features easily.

Assumption validity: (1) Market size: rough and self-admittedly unvalidated. (2) 15% conversion: unsupported; observed trial-to-paid is about 8% on a tiny sample, and free-trial users in a friendly local pilot overstate real-world conversion. (3) 100 paying vendors in 12 months contradicts the 180 local projection, and neither is tied to a funnel. (4) The problem evidence (17 of 23 use paper, 12 of 23 unsure on tax) is encouraging but is a small convenience sample near their own university and measures pain, not willingness to pay. (5) The $18,000 cost estimate for the year leaves almost no room for founder compensation and assumes founders' time is free at 15 hours/week each.

Strengths: Honest self-assessment; founder-market fit (family stall experience); a working product already built; real early users; a sensible use of funds that targets the right unknowns (legal setup, wider pilot, willingness-to-pay survey, retention).

Gaps and recommendations: Run pricing experiments (e.g., $5/$9/$15, annual prepay for seasonality) and measure paid retention across a full season; secure at least one market association partnership as a distribution test; decide whether to integrate payments (more defensible, higher revenue per vendor via processing fees) or stay a lightweight companion app; quantify CAC and time-to-payback; test the manager-reporting idea with actual quotes before relying on it; consider a lower-cost or seasonal plan to match vendor cash flow.

Overall: A credible, well-scoped pilot with genuine customer pain and an honest team, but not yet a validated business model. Revenue potential in the stated niche is modest, differentiation is thin, and key assumptions are untested. It is best viewed as a small, lean lifestyle-scale venture or a feature-sized product unless payments, multi-segment expansion, or partnership channels change the economics.
